goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:91 — Overriding all three role-mapping checks without honoring the caller's MANAGE_CLIENTS admin role can unexpectedly deny ordinary client administrators and break dependent admin operations.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the three role-mapping methods (canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, canMapClientScopeRoles) in ClientPermissionsV2.java delegate to hasPermission() which checks for specific schema permissions. The parent class ClientPermissions already handles the MANAGE_CLIENTS admin role check in its implementations. The V2 class is designed to add V2-specific permission checks, not replace the admin role checks entirely. The finding misreads the inheritance - these methods override the parent but the parent's canManage() method (which checks MANAGE_CLIENTS) is still available and used elsewhere in the permission flow. The V2 implementation is intentionally different for the fine-grained authorization feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — Enumerating only concrete authorization resources silently omits clients covered solely by a resource-type permission, so filtered bulk operations can act on a partial client set.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to getClientsWithPermission() at line 138 which iterates over resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE using resourceStore.findByType(). This only finds concrete client resources that have been explicitly created, not the resource-type permission that covers 'all clients'. Looking at hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope) method (lines 218-240), it properly handles both cases - first checking for a specific resource, then falling back to check the resource-type resource. However, getClientsWithPermission() does not have this fallback logic - it only iterates concrete resources. This means if a user has permission via a resource-type permission (covering all clients) but no specific client resources exist, getClientsWithPermission() would return an empty set even though the user actually has permission on all clients. This is a real correctness bug where the method returns incomplete results.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — A global Clients permission is ignored whenever the target client already has a resource created for any object-specific permission.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope) method at line 214, the logic is: first check if a resource exists for the specific client (line 213), if not found, then check for the 'all-clients' resource type permission (lines 215-220). However, if a resource DOES exist for the specific client (meaning someone created an object-specific permission for that client), the code proceeds to evaluate only that specific resource's permissions and never checks the global 'all-clients' permission. This means if ClientA has any object-specific permission defined, a user with global 'all-clients' MANAGE permission would not be able to manage ClientA unless they also have the specific permission. The correct behavior should be to check BOTH the specific resource permissions AND the global resource type permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — An existing client-specific resource prevents evaluation of the all-clients resource, so global grants are incorrectly denied for clients that have any specific permission.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope) method at line 214, when a client-specific resource exists (resourceStore.findByName returns non-null), the code immediately uses that resource for evaluation and never checks the all-clients resource. The code only falls through to check the all-clients resource (AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) when the client-specific resource is null. This means if a client has any specific permission defined, global grants on the all-clients resource would be ignored for that client, which is incorrect behavior - global permissions should still apply even when client-specific resources exist.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:67 — Existing admin-permissions clients are never backfilled with the new client scopes and all-clients resource because init returns immediately when the client already exists.

adjudication.rationale: The finding references 'init' method and backfilling behavior, but the diff does not show any 'init' method in AdminPermissionsSchema.java. The diff only shows: 1) Adding new constants (CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, CONFIGURE, MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE), 2) Creating a new CLIENTS ResourceType, 3) Adding CLIENTS to the schema Map in the constructor, 4) Adding resolveClient method. There is no 'init' method visible in this diff that would handle backfilling or early returns. The finding appears to reference code/behavior not shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:147 — Extending the legacy concrete evaluator forces ten inherited management APIs to become runtime UnsupportedOperationException traps, so V1 and V2 need a narrower shared boundary.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ClientPermissionsV2 extends ClientPermissions and overrides 10 methods (lines 147-195) to throw UnsupportedOperationException: exchangeToPermission, mapRolesPermission, mapRolesClientScopePermission, mapRolesCompositePermission, managePermission, configurePermission, viewPermission, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, and getPermissions. This is a legitimate architectural concern - the V2 implementation inherits from a concrete class but makes many inherited methods unusable at runtime. This creates a fragile design where callers of the interface could hit runtime exceptions. The finding correctly identifies that V1 and V2 should share a narrower interface rather than having V2 extend the full V1 implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:207 — Three near-identical permission-evaluation loops duplicate resource lookup and scope matching, making authorization behavior costly to change consistently.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that ClientPermissionsV2.java contains three very similar methods: hasPermission(ClientModel, String), hasPermission(String), and hasGrantedPermission(Resource, String) at lines 207-262. Each method performs similar resource lookup and permission evaluation with scope matching loops. This is a legitimate code duplication concern that could make future authorization behavior changes error-prone if one method is updated but others are not. However, this is a maintainability/refactoring concern rather than a bug - the code functions correctly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — Listing permitted clients scans every client resource and runs a separate authorization evaluation for each, so latency and database work grow linearly without pagination.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getClientsWithPermission() in ClientPermissionsV2.java (lines 127-142) iterates over all client resources using resourceStore.findByType() and calls hasGrantedPermission() for each one, which performs a separate authorization evaluation. This is a valid scalability/performance concern for the new code, though it's not a bug per se - the code will function correctly, just with O(n) authorization evaluations. This is a legitimate architectural concern about the implementation approach.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:359 — The role test grants MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, and CONFIGURE together, so it cannot detect one operation being authorized by the wrong client scope.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient grants MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, and CONFIGURE together in a single permission (line 359). This means the test cannot verify that each operation is authorized by its specific scope - for example, it cannot detect if addComposites() incorrectly checks MAP_ROLES instead of MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE. This is a valid test coverage concern for newly added permission logic, though it's a test quality issue rather than a bug in the production code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:64 — The new map-roles-client-scope permission has no integration test exercising either its allow or deny behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE as a new scope constant at line 64 and adds it to the CLIENTS ResourceType. The test file PermissionClientTest.java includes tests for MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE in testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient(), but there is no test that exercises MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE specifically. This is a valid observation about missing test coverage for newly added functionality - the canMapClientScopeRoles() method in ClientPermissionsV2 uses this scope but no test verifies its behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:208 — The explicit cross-realm denial paths for client permissions and filtered listings are untested, leaving this security boundary without regression coverage.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to line 208 in ClientPermissionsV2.java which contains the `hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope)` method that checks `if (!root.isAdminSameRealm()) { return false; }` - this is a cross-realm security check. Looking at the test file PermissionClientTest.java, the tests only cover same-realm scenarios (using realmAdminClient configured for the same realm). There are no tests that verify the cross-realm denial behavior where a user from a different realm attempts to access client permissions. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for a security-critical code path that was newly added in this diff.
